A working reference

Kinetic hierarchies: Liouville to Euler

How BBGKY, Vlasov, Fokker–Planck and the fluid equations are related — and why the same ladder, climbed in cosmology, fusion plasma and stellar dynamics, breaks in three different places.
Dr. Dipak Munshi  ·  Advanced Research Fellow, Imperial College London  ·  part of the ML & Stat Notes series
BBGKYVlasovFokker–Planck Boltzmannmoment closures cosmologyfusion / MHDstellar dynamics PM / P³M / TreePMMHD codesCMBPINNs

Abstract

There are two hierarchies in kinetic theory, not one, and they truncate in orthogonal directions: BBGKY cuts the chain of correlated particles, while the fluid reduction cuts the chain of velocity moments. Below both lie Newton, Liouville and BBGKY itself, all exact and all reversible; irreversibility appears only when a closure is imposed. Above them lie Vlasov, Boltzmann and Fokker–Planck as siblings, then continuity, Euler, viscosity and conduction. This note writes those relationships out explicitly, and then climbs the same ladder in three fields — large-scale structure, the tokamak edge, and stellar systems — to show that each fails in the same way and for the same reason, in the region where all the interesting physics lives.

Section 1 defines every quantity from the Hamiltonian up. The closing sections show how the kinetic equations are actually simulated (PM, P3M, TreePM and their MHD and plasma counterparts, with pointers into public source code), where the CMB sits on the same ladder, and how physics-informed neural networks are implemented on it, with worked, trained examples including three from MHD. Section 12 treats effective field theory as the systematic version of every closure, comparing n-point and field-level inference and where PINNs help. Appendix A derives the key results; Appendix B points to the code that reproduces every figure and animation.

1First principles: every quantity, defined

Everything later on this page is built from the objects on this one. Nothing else is assumed.

The system and its Hamiltonian

Take identical point particles, each of mass (and charge , if charged). Particle has position and momentum , where is its velocity. All the physics is in one function, the Hamiltonian — the total energy written in terms of these coordinates:

The three terms are kinetic energy, the pair potential (written for particles 1 and 2) between every pair of particles a distance apart, and any external potential . The two force laws on this page are

with Newton’s constant and the permittivity of free space. Equal masses always attract; equal charges repel. That one sign is the origin of most of the differences in Section 7.

The motion follows from Hamilton’s equations,

which is just Newton’s second law. This is level one: coupled ordinary differential equations.

Phase space and Liouville’s theorem

Collect all coordinates into one point in a -dimensional phase space. The whole system is one point moving with velocity . Its divergence vanishes identically, because mixed second derivatives commute:

So the flow in phase space is incompressible (Liouville’s theorem). Now suppose we do not know the exact state, only a probability density , normalised so that . Probability is conserved, so it obeys a continuity equation in phase space, , and incompressibility turns this into the Liouville equation:

In words: probability density is constant along every trajectory, . This is level two.

Reduced distributions and the BBGKY step

Nobody needs all coordinates. The -particle distribution keeps particles and integrates the rest away. From here on we use velocity instead of momentum and write :

With this normalisation, is the expected number of particles in the small phase-space box , and the expected number of pairs. Integrating the Liouville equation over particles gives an equation for in which, because forces are pairwise, appears — that chain is BBGKY (level three, Section 3). The pair correlation measures how far the pair distribution is from two independent particles,

and is the analogous three-particle part. The mean-field force is what a particle at feels from the average density of all the others,

For gravity this is , where the gravitational potential solves Poisson’s equation with mass density . For charges the same role is played by the electrostatic potential , with and the charge density.

The kinetic equation, generically

Every kinetic equation on this page has the same skeleton, with the smooth (mean-field plus external) acceleration ( for gravity, for charges):

Here . The left side moves along smooth orbits; the collision operator is everything the smooth field misses — the effect of . Whatever form it takes, an elastic collision operator conserves particle number, momentum and energy:

Its unique fixed point, the distribution that collisions leave unchanged, is the Maxwellian

where is Boltzmann’s constant, and , , are the density, mean velocity and temperature defined as moments in Section 5.

2Two hierarchies, not one

An equation’s place on one ladder says nothing about its place on the other.

Most of the confusion in this subject comes from running two separate ladders together. One truncates in how many particles are correlated; the other in which velocity moment of the single-particle distribution you keep. They are independent, so you can be collisionless and fluid, or kinetic and collisional, in any combination.

Correlation axis — BBGKY

The chain
— the equation for contains
Vlasov: the mean field
to
Boltzmann (short range, hard) or Lenard–Balescu → Landau–Fokker–Planck (long range, screened)

Moment axis — fluid reduction

continuity — density
momentum — Euler, Navier–Stokes, Braginskii
pressure and stress — viscosity
heat flux — thermal conduction

So Vlasov and Braginskii are not rungs of one ladder. One is a correlation closure of the pair distribution; the other is a moment closure of the single-particle distribution.

3Going down: the exact levels

Below the kinetic equations, classically, there are three levels — and the lowest two carry the same content. The microscopic dynamics is simply Newton for interacting particles,

which is what molecular dynamics and direct -body integration actually solve. The same dynamics written for the -particle distribution is the Liouville equation — an incompressible flow of probability density in -dimensional phase space,

Integrating out particles gives the reduced -particle distributions,

and the chain of equations they obey is BBGKY. Nothing has been approximated at any of these three levels: the information content is identical, and the only change is bookkeeping.

The structural fact

All three exact levels are time-reversible: send , and every equation above is unchanged. Irreversibility does not exist anywhere below the closure — it appears at the moment you assert something about that you cannot derive. Boltzmann’s H-theorem follows from molecular chaos, not from the mechanics.

4Closing the first link

The first member of the BBGKY chain is an equation for whose right-hand side still contains . For a pair potential it reads

Now split the pair distribution into an uncorrelated product plus a genuine two-particle correlation,

and the single interaction term splits in two. The product piece contributes

which is not a collision at all but a smooth force from the average density, so it belongs on the left-hand side. What remains on the right, built from , is the collision operator. Three closures follow.

Vlasov: set

One assumption — statistical independence — simultaneously creates the mean field and removes the collisions, because a particle that knows nothing about individual neighbours can only respond to their average. For a plasma the mean field is electromagnetic and the result is Vlasov–Maxwell:

closed self-consistently because the sources of the fields are moments of itself,

and in the electrostatic limit the field equation collapses to a single Poisson solve, . The gravitational twin, Vlasov–Poisson, is

The two differ by a constant, a sign, and the fact that always.

Boltzmann: to first order, short-ranged and hard

With molecular chaos for the incoming pair, plus the dilute, local and instantaneous assumptions, the collision term becomes the Boltzmann integral — gain minus loss over all scattering angles,

where primes denote post-collision velocities.

Landau–Fokker–Planck: to first order, long-ranged and screened

Here you cannot stop at the first equation. Close the second BBGKY equation by setting the three-particle correlation , solve it for at fixed (assuming relaxes fast), and substitute back. The result is the Lenard–Balescu operator, in which screening enters through the plasma dielectric function ; replacing that dynamical screening by its static Debye form reduces it to the Landau–Fokker–Planck operator.

Boltzmann and Fokker–Planck are therefore siblings, not rungs: two closures of the same equation under different interaction assumptions, each first order in its own small parameter — the dilute-gas density for one, for the other. Vlasov sits below both, being zeroth order.

Fokker–Planck as the small-angle limit of Boltzmann

The same operator can be reached from Boltzmann directly, and that route explains the Coulomb logarithm. Rewrite the collision integral exactly as a master equation, with the rate of collisions that change the velocity by :

Assume is small and Taylor-expand the gain term about . The zeroth-order terms cancel against the loss term, and truncating at second order — which is the approximation — leaves a drift–diffusion equation in velocity space,

whose coefficients are the first two moments of the transition rate,

The first is dynamical friction, the second the velocity-diffusion tensor. Evaluate them with a Rutherford cross-section: a collision at impact parameter gives while the number of such collisions goes as , so both moments reduce to

In a plasma the upper cutoff is screening and the lower is the hard-deflection radius,

That logarithm, – in a fusion plasma, is the fingerprint of an effect to which every decade of impact parameter contributes equally. In a stellar system the same integral appears with the size of the system and .

5Going up: the moment ladder

Define the moments of in the usual way — number density, mean velocity, pressure tensor and heat flux,

Taking successive velocity moments of whichever kinetic equation you have then gives continuity,

and momentum,

in which the momentum equation contains the second moment , whose own equation contains the third moment , and so on. The chain is unclosed in exactly the way BBGKY is.

Elastic collisions conserve particle number, momentum and energy, so for a single species : the collision term drops out of the first moments altogether, and Vlasov and Boltzmann give the identical continuity and momentum equations. Collisions enter in two other ways — between species, as friction and temperature equilibration, which is where resistivity comes from; and, far more importantly, by setting the closure, since Chapman–Enskog computes and from the collision operator itself. Reactions are the exception: ionisation, recombination and charge exchange are not elastic, so they appear as source terms at zeroth moment.

Euler
and : an ideal fluid, .

Both supplied at first order in Chapman–Enskog,

The magnetised version of the same step, with and split into parallel, perpendicular and gyro components, plus thermoelectric cross-terms.
Burnett
Second order in the expansion. Known to be unstable at short wavelengths, so rarely used in practice.
Grad 13-moment
Gives and their own evolution equations instead of constitutive formulae. Loses hyperbolicity far from equilibrium.

Below all of these sit further asymptotic reductions — gyrokinetics, drift-kinetics, MHD, Grad–Shafranov — which remove fast timescales rather than high moments.

6Collisional and collisionless, in general

The distinction is not a property of a system but an ordering between two timescales, or equivalently two lengths:

For Coulomb collisions the Rutherford cross-section goes as , which makes both ratios strongly temperature-dependent,

so a hot plasma is nearly collisionless and a cold one collisional, with no change in the physics other than temperature. For a self-gravitating system of bodies the equivalent statement is

so collisionality is controlled by rather than by temperature.

Collisionless means nothing drives towards a Maxwellian, so there is no local thermodynamic equilibrium and no reason for the distribution to have any particular shape: can stay anisotropic, multi-humped or carry a non-thermal tail indefinitely. Phase-space structure survives, including filamentation and multi-streaming, and entropy is conserved. Fluid closures then need extra care: they can still be very useful, but their coefficients must come from kinetic theory or simulation rather than from a Chapman–Enskog expansion. Collisional means the operator relaxes towards a Maxwellian faster than the macroscopic flow changes, which is precisely what makes a fluid description possible and what Chapman–Enskog expands in.

The hard cases are in between, where : the closure has no derivation, and the practical answer is a fitted parameter or a direct kinetic simulation. Every field has such a region.

7The same ladder in three fields

What changes is the force law — its range, its sign, whether it screens — and the number of particles. Everything else follows.

Case one — cosmology: large-scale structure

Gravity is unscreened, its source is positive-definite, and is effectively infinite, so vastly exceeds the age of the universe. Dark matter is collisionless to an excellent approximation and the governing equation is Vlasov–Poisson. In comoving coordinates with conformal time , the first two moments are

and standard perturbation theory closes them by discarding the velocity-dispersion tensor entirely, — the single-stream, pressureless perfect fluid. It fails at shell crossing: once orbits cross, multi-streaming generates dispersion and vorticity the closure cannot represent, which is why perturbation theory has irrotational flow for all time and breaks down exactly where structure forms.

The repairs are frank about being repairs. The adhesion model adds an artificial viscosity and turns Euler into Burgers’ equation, ; the effective field theory of large-scale structure restores the discarded stress as a counterterm with fitted coefficients,

Numerically the field turned to direct simulation — and note the subtlety: a particle-mesh code integrates Newton’s equations, level one, while the thing it represents is Vlasov. Softening keeps that correspondence honest by suppressing a collisionality the discretisation would otherwise introduce, replacing the point-mass potential by, for example, . Because gravity does not screen, the mesh force alone is insufficient at small scales, so a short-range stage is bolted on: direct pair summation in , a multipole tree in TreePM, or mesh refinement in AMR.

Case two — fusion plasma and MHD

Two signs of charge change everything. Beyond a charge is screened, the potential becoming Yukawa rather than Coulomb,

and any region larger than is quasineutral, so distant monopoles cancel and there is no long-range pairwise force at all. The mesh carries the collective self-consistent field at scales ; below nothing collective survives, only collisions. That is why a plasma code has no short-range pair stage and needs no tree.

The kinetic equation is Vlasov–Maxwell with the Landau collision operator restored,

usually in electrostatic form, since is dominated by the external coils. Collisionality scales as , so the same device holds both regimes: the hot core is effectively collisionless and treated with the gyrokinetic reduction, while the cold dense edge and divertor are genuinely collisional, needing Fokker–Planck for the charged species and a kinetic treatment for the neutrals, which exist only there — in practice a Monte Carlo neutral code such as EIRENE, coupled to the plasma solver.

The magnetic field makes transport violently anisotropic. Along particles stream freely over ; across it they random-walk by a gyroradius per collision, so

That single ratio is why the scrape-off layer is millimetres thick and why the exhaust is funnelled onto the divertor. Charge also brings coefficients with no neutral-gas analogue: resistivity, gyroviscosity, and thermoelectric cross-terms coupling heat flux to current.

The closure fails in the scrape-off layer, where can exceed the connection length. The symptom is the Spitzer–Härm flux exceeding what free streaming could carry, ; the standard remedy is a flux limiter

whose coefficient is set by comparison with kinetic calculations. A great deal of careful work goes into doing better than this: UKAEA’s ReMKiT1D framework, for example, couples fluid models of the scrape-off layer to a kinetic treatment of the electrons, so the heat-flux closure is computed rather than assumed. Cross-field transport, meanwhile, is set mainly by drift-wave turbulence rather than by the collisional coefficients, which is why turbulence codes such as BOUT++ and Hermes-3 are central to edge modelling.

and even there the pressure and current profiles must be supplied from outside. In practice fusion modelling uses every rung of the ladder together, and does so with real sophistication: fluid edge codes coupled to kinetic Monte Carlo neutrals carry design studies, gyrokinetic and kinetic codes supply and test the closures, and frameworks that couple fluid, particle and kinetic-neutral models in one calculation — the aim of UKAEA’s exascale Project NEPTUNE — are where the frontier now is.

Sign and normalisation conventions for differ between texts.

The UK fusion programme on this ladder

Few organisations work on every rung of this hierarchy at once. The UK Atomic Energy Authority does, from experiment to equilibrium to kinetic theory, and much of its software is openly available.

  • Experiment. UKAEA operated JET at Culham for its European partners until the end of 2023; its final deuterium–tritium campaign set a world record of 69 MJ of fusion energy from 0.2 mg of fuel. MAST Upgrade tests the Super-X divertor, an exhaust geometry designed to spread and cool the heat load — the scrape-off-layer problem of this section, attacked through magnetic geometry.
  • Equilibrium (the Grad–Shafranov rung). FreeGSNKE, developed by UKAEA with the STFC Hartree Centre, extends FreeGS to static and evolutive free-boundary equilibria and carries a full MAST-U machine description.
  • Fluid–kinetic coupling (the closure problem itself). ReMKiT1D builds reactive multi-fluid models of the scrape-off layer with coupled electron kinetics: precisely the step this page describes, a moment closure informed directly by the kinetic equation.
  • Exascale edge physics. UKAEA’s Project NEPTUNE (NEutrals & Plasma TUrbulence Numerics for the Exascale), part of the ExCALIBUR programme, develops coupled fluid, particle and kinetic-neutral methods for the edge, with open code such as NESO and NESO-Particles — the particle–mesh ideas of Section 9 rebuilt for the next generation of supercomputers.
  • Turbulence and power plants. Edge turbulence work uses BOUT++ and Hermes-3; the systems code PROCESS ties the physics to whole-plant design, the scale at which the STEP prototype power plant is being developed.

It is a striking example of the theme of this note done well: every level of description kept, each used where it is valid, and each checked against the one below it.

Case three — galactic dynamics and star clusters

Gravity again, unscreened and single-signed, but now is small: in a galaxy, only – in a globular cluster. Since , the same force law gives opposite answers in the two cases — and this is the field where both branches of the hierarchy are used in earnest.

A galaxy is collisionless, and the governing equation is the collisionless Boltzmann equation — Vlasov under its stellar-dynamical name,

Its moment reduction gives the Jeans equations,

which are explicitly unclosed. In the spherical steady state they become

so the anisotropy parameter must be assumed — which is the origin of the mass–anisotropy degeneracy, and the same species of thing as a flux limiter: an unclosed moment equation patched by a fitted parameter.

A globular cluster is collisional: is shorter than its age, so two-body encounters drive real physics — mass segregation, core collapse, evaporation, binary hardening. The tool is Fokker–Planck, often orbit-averaged, and Chandrasekhar’s dynamical friction formula is precisely its drift coefficient :

complete with the same Coulomb logarithm, here with .

Dynamical friction, live. The same 3000 stars and the same heavy body (4% of the halo mass), run twice. The body pulls a wake of stars behind it, the wake pulls back, and the body spirals in — Chandrasekhar’s drift term at work. With softening (smaller than the strong-deflection radius ) close encounters keep their full strength; with they are smoothed away, drops from to , and the body sinks several times more slowly. Softening is right for a collisionless cosmological code and wrong for a star cluster. Restricted N-body: the stars move in a fixed Plummer potential and feel the body; the body feels every star.

The numerical contrast with cosmology is the sharpest illustration of the whole argument. Cosmological codes soften the force to suppress two-body relaxation, because collisionality there is a numerical artefact. Direct -body cluster codes do not soften, because collisionality is the physics. Same equations, same algorithms, opposite intent.

There is also a phenomenon with no analogue in the other two cases: violent relaxation, in which a collisionless system reaches quasi-equilibrium through the time-varying collective potential rather than through encounters — relaxation without collisions.

9Simulations: how the kinetic equation is actually solved

Every method below is the same trick with a different force solver, and every MHD code is the same trick one rung further up the moment ladder.

The one idea: sample with particles

A six-dimensional grid for is usually too expensive, so instead we represent by macro-particles (much fewer than the real ), each carrying a mass :

Substitute this into the Vlasov equation and it is satisfied exactly provided each sample point moves along a characteristic — that is, obeys Newton’s law in the mean field:

So a simulation looks like level one (Newton for many bodies) but represents level four (Vlasov). The price is that makes each macro-particle far heavier than a real particle, which would create spurious two-body collisions; smoothing each particle over a finite size — softening in gravity, shape functions in plasma — removes them. All the methods below differ only in how the force is computed from the particles.

Method 1 — Particle–Mesh (PM)

Put a regular grid of spacing over the box and do four steps every time-step.

(a) Assign mass to the grid. Each particle shares its mass among nearby cells with a weight ; the common cloud-in-cell (CIC) choice is linear in each direction:

(b) Solve Poisson by FFT. In Fourier space the Laplacian is multiplication by , so

where denotes a Fourier transform and . In an expanding universe with comoving coordinates, is replaced by (Section 7, case one).

(c) Differentiate, , or by finite differences on the grid. (d) Interpolate back to each particle with the same (this guarantees no particle pushes on itself) and advance with the leapfrog (kick–drift–kick) integrator,

which is symplectic — it respects the phase-space incompressibility of Section 1, so energy errors stay bounded instead of drifting. The cost is for grid cells: very fast. The weakness is resolution: forces are wrong below about , which is fatal inside a dense halo.

Method 2 — P3M (particle–particle/particle–mesh)

Keep PM for the long-range force and add back what the mesh missed, by direct summation over close neighbours inside a cut-off radius of a few cells:

Accurate, but the direct sum costs (number of particles) × (neighbours within ), and gravity makes things cluster, so the cost explodes as structure forms. The classic fix (adaptive P3M) puts finer meshes inside dense regions — a step towards AMR.

Method 3 — Tree, FMM and TreePM: the multipole route (GADGET)

A distant clump of particles, seen from far away, looks like a single point — plus small corrections. That is a multipole expansion. For a group of total mass at centre of mass , at separation ,

The first term is the monopole, the quadrupole tensor, and the dipole vanishes because we expand about the centre of mass. A Barnes–Hut tree nests the box into cubes of side and uses a cube’s multipoles whenever it looks small enough, (the opening angle, typically 0.5–0.7); otherwise it opens the cube and looks at its children. Cost: , with resolution that follows the particles automatically. The fast multipole method (FMM) also expands at the receiving end, so whole groups interact with whole groups: .

TreePM combines the two by splitting the potential with a smooth filter of width : a Gaussian cut in Fourier space for the long-range part, solved on the mesh,

and the complementary short-range part, which dies off within a few , from the tree. This is the default in GADGET-2; GADGET-4 offers tree, FMM, TreePM and pure PM as compile-time options. Periodic boundaries come free with the FFT — one reason TreePM displaced pure trees in cosmology.

The plasma counterparts

Particle-in-cell (PIC) is PM for plasma. Deposit charge and current to the grid with a shape function, solve the field equations, interpolate back, push. In electrostatic PIC the field solve is — the gravitational FFT with the sign flipped. In electromagnetic PIC it is Maxwell’s equations advanced on a staggered (Yee) grid,

and the particle push uses the Boris scheme, which rotates about exactly. Why no tree or P3M stage? Because of Debye screening (Section 7, case two): beyond there is no long-range pairwise force left for the mesh to miss, so collisions are added stochastically (Monte Carlo binary collisions) instead.

Two-stream instability, electrostatic PIC. 20 000 electrons in two counter-streaming beams (green moving left, blue right) on a neutralising ion background: exactly PM with the sign of the force flipped — cloud-in-cell deposit, Gauss’s law , leapfrog push. A tiny ripple grows exponentially (the straight line on the right, in log scale), then the beams trap each other and roll up into phase-space vortices. This is the plasma twin of shell crossing: multi-streaming in that no fluid closure can represent. Moving the slider changes the beam speed and restarts.

The exceptions prove the rule. When there are few particles per Debye sphere (: strongly coupled, dusty or ultracold plasmas, ions in molecular dynamics), screening fails and the gravitational toolkit returns unchanged: P3M for charges is called PPPM (it is the standard long-range solver in LAMMPS), and the Barnes–Hut tree for Coulomb forces is PEPC.

The MHD variants: one rung up the moment ladder

MHD is what you get by taking the moments of Section 5 for electrons and ions, adding them, assuming quasineutrality, and using Ohm’s law (with resistivity , zero in ideal MHD). In conservation form, with self-gravity included as a source:

where is the total energy density, the adiabatic index and the unit tensor. The magnetic terms add a pressure and a tension along field lines.

The key contrast, in one line

Gravity is elliptic; MHD is hyperbolic. Poisson’s equation has no time derivative: every mass feels every other mass instantly, which is why it needs a global solver — FFT, tree or FMM. The MHD equations carry information at finite speeds — sound and Alfvén — so each cell only talks to its neighbours. MHD is solved locally (Godunov schemes with Riemann solvers), with a time-step limited by the Courant condition

with the fast magnetosonic speed and . A cosmological MHD code is therefore always two codes glued together: a PM/TreePM gravity solver plus a local MHD solver, coupled through the source term .

How the multipole idea connects to MHD. The magnetic field produced by currents is also a long-range field (Biot–Savart), and could in principle be summed with a tree, exactly like gravity. MHD avoids this by evolving itself through the local induction equation, so no tree is needed for the field. The one non-local piece left is the constraint , which numerical errors break. There are two remedies, and they mirror the two families of gravity solver:

  • Mesh codes → constrained transport. Store on cell faces and update it from edge electric fields; then stays zero to round-off. Alternatively, project: with — which is the same FFT Poisson solve as PM. (RAMSES, Athena++, Enzo.)
  • Particle codes → divergence cleaning. SPH-MHD (the GADGET family) and meshless MHD (GIZMO) cannot use face-centred fields, so they carry away as a damped wave (Dedner cleaning) or subtract its effect (Powell source terms). AREPO’s moving mesh sits between the two and has used both.

Orszag–Tang vortex, ideal MHD. The standard test: smooth vortical flow and field on a periodic box steepen into interacting shocks and a central current sheet by . Solved here with the equations of this section — Rusanov fluxes, second-order reconstruction, RK2, Courant-limited time-step — with one twist: is computed from a vector potential, , and is simply advected with the flow. In 2D that makes exactly, which is the idea behind constrained transport. Each cell only ever talks to its neighbours: hyperbolic, local, no tree.

The same vortex in three dimensions

The 2D animation above is a slice of a richer problem. In 3D the field is computed from a three-component vector potential, , advected in the gauge , so again stays at round-off. A small resistivity, , keeps the sheets resolved on the grid. Adding a field component that varies along , with , couples the planes: the flat current sheets of 2D twist and fragment into a three-dimensional web. A run at 643 to takes about 2 minutes on a laptop in Python; the max-projection of shows the sheets through the whole box.

Three checks keep it honest: with every -plane reproduces the 2D vortex exactly; stays below ; and total energy, which the conservative scheme guarantees, drifts by less than . Kinetic and magnetic energy exchange while grows as the sheets steepen — the route to the dissipation that resistive MHD codes must resolve.

Reproduce with sims/orszag_tang_3d.py (--n sets the grid; 1283 is about 16× the work of 643 and suits an HPC node).

So the map is: PM mesh ↔ grid MHD with constrained transport; tree/SPH particles ↔ SPH-MHD with cleaning; and in plasma physics proper, PIC ↔ kinetic, MHD/Braginskii codes ↔ fluid.

10Where the CMB sits

The photons of the early universe climb the whole ladder in time: a collisional fluid before recombination, a collisionless Vlasov gas after it.

The cosmic microwave background is the cleanest application of everything on this page, because the perturbations are small and every equation can be linearised. Each species gets its own kinetic equation on the same expanding background:

  • Cold dark matter — collisionless and cold: only the moments (density and velocity) are needed. This is the pressureless fluid closure of Section 7, case one, before shell crossing.
  • Neutrinos — collisionless after about one second: the linearised Vlasov equation.
  • Photons — the full linearised Boltzmann equation, with Thomson scattering off free electrons as the collision operator.
  • Baryons — a fluid, tied to the photons by that same scattering.

The photon Boltzmann equation

Describe the photons by their fractional temperature perturbation , as a function of conformal time , Fourier wavenumber , and the cosine between the wave and the photon direction. The metric is , with and the two gravitational potentials (in this section only, following Dodelson’s textbook). Ignoring polarisation,

A dot is ; is the baryon velocity; is the second Legendre polynomial; and the opacity is the scattering rate per unit conformal time, with the free electron density and the Thomson cross-section. Its inverse is the photon mean free path. The left side is exactly the Vlasov operator of Section 1 in an expanding universe; the right side is , and it pushes towards isotropy in the electron rest frame.

It is the moment ladder

Expand in Legendre polynomials, . Each multipole is a velocity moment: is the density (monopole), the velocity (dipole), the anisotropic stress (quadrupole) — the same , , as Section 5. Substituting gives, for ,

an infinite chain in which every moment drives the next one up — unclosed in precisely the way of Section 5. Boltzmann codes truncate it at some with a free-streaming closure for : a moment closure, nothing more.

Before recombination: collisional, so a fluid

The relevant Knudsen number is , the photon mean free path over the wavelength. Before recombination () it is tiny, and the collision term forces : photons and baryons move as one tightly coupled fluid. The monopole then obeys a driven, damped oscillator,

whose sound speed (in units of ) sets the acoustic peaks. This is the Euler rung for the photon–baryon fluid.

Go to first order in — exactly the Chapman–Enskog step that turns Euler into Navier–Stokes — and the photons acquire a viscosity and a heat conduction. Their effect is Silk damping: photons random-walk out of small-scale waves and erase them. The damping length is the random-walk distance, roughly

the geometric mean of the mean free path and the horizon, which is why the CMB spectrum falls off beyond .

Sound waves before recombination (toy). A patch of the photon–baryon fluid with scale-invariant initial potentials. Every Fourier mode oscillates as (the matter-era tight-coupling solution of Hu & Sugiyama), with sound horizon growing in time and the Silk scale shrinking as photons random-walk further. At recombination () the pattern freezes: modes caught at an extremum make the peaks, those caught at a node the troughs, and the smallest scales are damped away. Raise and the odd (compression) peaks grow relative to the even ones — the baryon signature Planck measures. A 2D patch and a schematic map, not a Boltzmann-code calculation.

After recombination: collisionless, so Vlasov

When the electrons combine into atoms, drops to almost zero and the photons free-stream. The ladder now transfers power upward without loss: a pattern at wavenumber on the last-scattering surface, at distance , appears on the sky at multipole . Formally,

with a spherical Bessel function. This line-of-sight solution is the trick that made modern Boltzmann codes fast: integrate the ladder only to a modest , then project. The angular power spectrum follows from the primordial curvature spectrum ,

where is today per unit initial curvature perturbation (normalisation conventions vary).

The Fokker–Planck rung: spectral distortions

Everything above concerns the direction of photons. Their energy spectrum is changed by Compton scattering off hot electrons, where each scattering shifts the energy only slightly. Taking the small-shift limit of the Compton Boltzmann integral — exactly the small-angle step that gave Fokker–Planck in Section 4 — gives the Kompaneets equation for the photon occupation number :

The derivative term is diffusion in energy, is recoil, is stimulated scattering; is the Compton -parameter. It describes both the - and -type distortions of the CMB spectrum and the Sunyaev–Zel’dovich effect in galaxy clusters.

11Physics-informed neural networks

A PINN replaces the grid by a neural network and the solver by an optimiser. Its natural job on this ladder is to learn the closure parameters that every field ends up fitting.

The idea

Write any equation on this page as , where is the unknown field (a density, a velocity, itself) and the differential operator. Represent by a neural network with weights . Because the network is a smooth function, automatic differentiation gives , , exactly, and so the residual can be evaluated at any point. Training minimises

where the residual is evaluated at randomly placed collocation points — no mesh. The last term is what makes PINNs interesting: an unknown coefficient in can be made a trainable parameter alongside , and the data then determine it. That is an inverse problem.

Worked example: learning the adhesion viscosity

Take the adhesion model of Section 7, case one — Euler with an artificial viscosity, i.e. Burgers’ equation, the one-dimensional prototype of a closure with a fitted coefficient:

Pretend is unknown. Generate 200 scattered “observations” from the exact solution with (via the Cole–Hopf transform) plus 1% noise, start the network at , and train on the loss above with 4000 collocation points: 6000 Adam steps followed by L-BFGS, about a minute on a laptop CPU.

Training, replayed. 53 snapshots from the same run: the network’s solution at three times (solid) against the exact answer (dashed), and the viscosity it infers. Early on the network fits the data points but not the equation; as the residual term takes hold the shock sharpens and is dragged down to the value the physics requires. Drag the slider to scrub.

The network recovers the viscosity to 0.3% and the whole space–time solution, including the steepening shock at , to about 0.2%. The core of the implementation is short:

import torch, numpy as np

net = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 32), torch.nn.Tanh(),     # u_theta(t, x)
                          torch.nn.Linear(32, 32), torch.nn.Tanh(),
                          torch.nn.Linear(32, 32), torch.nn.Tanh(),
                          torch.nn.Linear(32, 32), torch.nn.Tanh(),
                          torch.nn.Linear(32, 1))
log_nu = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(np.log(0.1)))   # the unknown closure coefficient
u = lambda t, x: net(torch.cat([t, x], 1))
d = lambda y, z: torch.autograd.grad(y, z, torch.ones_like(y), create_graph=True)[0]

def residual(t, x):                                       # u_t + u u_x - nu u_xx
    t.requires_grad_(True); x.requires_grad_(True)
    uu = u(t, x); ux = d(uu, x)
    return d(uu, t) + uu * ux - torch.exp(log_nu) * d(ux, x)

def loss():   # tf, xf: collocation; x0: t=0 line; tb, xb: x=+-1; td, xd, ud: observations
    return (residual(tf, xf).pow(2).mean()
            + (u(0 * x0, x0) + torch.sin(np.pi * x0)).pow(2).mean()
            + u(tb, xb).pow(2).mean()
            + (u(td, xd) - ud).pow(2).mean())

opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(net.parameters()) + [log_nu], lr=2e-3)
for it in range(6000):
    opt.zero_grad(); L = loss(); L.backward(); opt.step()
# ...then polish with torch.optim.LBFGS; read off torch.exp(log_nu)

The full script, including the exact solution and the scoring, is code/kinetic_hierarchies/pinn/burgers_inverse.py.

Going down the ladder: a Vlasov–Poisson PINN

The same recipe applies to the kinetic level. For electrons on a fixed ion background in one space and one velocity dimension (plasma units), Vlasov–Poisson is

Two networks are needed, and , and the only new ingredient is the velocity integral in Gauss’s law, done by quadrature over on a fixed set of -nodes:

import torch, numpy as np
# 1D-1V electrostatic Vlasov-Poisson for electrons on a fixed ion background (plasma units):
#   f_t + v f_x - E f_v = 0,     E_x = 1 - \int f dv
mlp = lambda n_in: torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(n_in, 64), torch.nn.Tanh(),
                                       torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))
f_net, E_net = mlp(3), mlp(2)                       # f(t,x,v) and E(t,x): two networks
vq, wq = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(64)        # quadrature in v on [-6, 6]
vq = torch.tensor(6 * vq, dtype=torch.float32); wq = torch.tensor(6 * wq, dtype=torch.float32)
d = lambda y, z: torch.autograd.grad(y, z, torch.ones_like(y), create_graph=True)[0]

def residuals(t, x, v):
    t.requires_grad_(True); x.requires_grad_(True); v.requires_grad_(True)
    f = f_net(torch.cat([t, x, v], 1)); E = E_net(torch.cat([t, x], 1))
    r_vlasov = d(f, t) + v * d(f, x) - E * d(f, v)
    # density n(t,x) = \int f dv by Gauss-Legendre: evaluate f on the v-nodes at each (t,x)
    tq, xq = t.repeat_interleave(64, 0), x.repeat_interleave(64, 0)
    fq = f_net(torch.cat([tq, xq, vq.repeat(len(t))[:, None]], 1)).view(-1, 64)
    n = (fq * wq).sum(1, keepdim=True)
    r_poisson = d(E, x) - (1 - n)
    return r_vlasov, r_poisson

# one training step (initial and periodic-boundary losses omitted for brevity)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(f_net.parameters()) + list(E_net.parameters()), lr=1e-3)
for step in range(5):
    t = torch.rand(512, 1) * 20; x = torch.rand(512, 1) * 4 * np.pi; v = (torch.rand(512, 1) - .5) * 12
    rv, rp = residuals(t, x, v)
    loss = rv.pow(2).mean() + rp.pow(2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    print(step, float(loss))

This runs, but it shows at once why PINNs have not replaced PIC. The input space is dimensional (seven for real problems); collisionless develops ever-finer filaments in velocity, which networks are slow to learn (“spectral bias”); and conservation of mass and energy is only as good as the loss, not built in, as it is in a symplectic particle code.

MHD examples: three inverse problems from the fluid end of the ladder

The same machinery applies directly to MHD, and the most useful PINNs there are inverse problems: a few measurements, a known equation, and an unknown physical parameter. All three examples below were trained for this page and are scored against exact solutions (derived in Appendix A.7 and A.11). Each runs in seconds to a couple of minutes on a laptop CPU.

1. Equilibrium reconstruction: Grad–Shafranov

Tokamak equilibrium reconstruction — the job done routinely by codes such as EFIT — infers the pressure and current profiles from magnetic measurements by solving the Grad–Shafranov equation. Here is the PINN version on a Solov’ev equilibrium:

The network sees the flux on the boundary of the box (as from flux loops) and 40 noisy interior samples; the residual is enforced at 3000 collocation points, with trained alongside the weights from a starting guess of 0.5.

2. A damped Alfvén wave: learning and the resistivity

Transverse perturbations of a uniform field obey the linearised MHD pair

with the magnetic diffusivity (taken equal to the kinematic viscosity). Both the Alfvén speed and are unknown. A two-output network is trained on 300 noisy samples of each field; periodicity is built in exactly by feeding the network instead of — a small trick that removes the boundary loss altogether.

3. Hartmann flow: measuring the field from the flow

A conducting fluid pushed along a channel across a magnetic field is braked by , which flattens the parabolic profile and squeezes the shear into thin Hartmann layers of thickness :

From 25 noisy velocity samples the PINN recovers the profile and the Hartmann number, i.e. the field strength. The wall boundary condition is imposed exactly by writing — the second standard trick, alongside built-in periodicity.

What these show. In each case the physics residual does the heavy lifting: 25–300 noisy points would never pin down a field and a coefficient on their own, but together with the equation they determine both to better than a percent. The same structure, with real diagnostics and a full equilibrium or transport model, is what makes PINNs attractive for reconstruction and for calibrating closures in fusion and astrophysical plasmas. The caveats from the Vlasov example still apply: stiff boundary layers (large Ha), shocks and multi-scale turbulence remain hard, and the conservation properties of a good finite-volume or particle code are not inherited.

Where PINNs are actually useful here

  • Inverse problems and closure parameters. Every field in Section 7 ended with a fitted number — the EFT , the flux limiter , the anisotropy . A PINN fits such a parameter with the equation enforced everywhere, not just at the data points, exactly as with above.
  • Sparse or irregular data. Diagnostics in a tokamak edge, or tracers in a halo, sample the field at a few points; the residual term fills the gaps physically.
  • Learned closures. A related idea replaces a constitutive law (say or in Section 5) by a small network trained on kinetic simulations. That is not strictly a PINN, but it is the same move: keep the moment equations, learn the closure.
  • The CMB is the counter-example. Linear Boltzmann codes are already fast and accurate, so the machine-learning effort there goes into emulators such as CosmoPower, which learn the map from cosmological parameters to rather than solving the equations.

Source code. The original PINN code, maziarraissi/PINNs: its appendix/continuous_time_identification (Burgers)/ example is the inverse problem above. DeepXDE is the most complete general library: see examples/pinn_forward/Burgers.py and the examples/pinn_inverse/ folder. NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo (formerly Modulus) is the industrial-scale option. In this series, the PINN notes cover the theory, training and failure modes in detail.

12Effective field theory: the closure made systematic

Every closure on this page answers one question: what do you put in for the stress you cannot compute? EFT answers it by listing everything symmetry allows and measuring the coefficients.

12.1 Smoothing, and the stress it leaves behind

Take the Vlasov–Poisson system of Section 7 (cosmology) and smooth every field with a filter that removes wavenumbers above a cut-off , chosen below the nonlinear scale : , . The moment equations (Appendix A.4) for the long-wavelength fields keep their form, except for one new term (conformal time , ):

The effective stress is everything the short modes do to the long ones. It has two parts:

The first is the second velocity moment that standard perturbation theory sets to zero (Section 5). The second is built from short-wavelength potential gradients: it is the cosmological counterpart of the pair correlation . So EFT is a coarse-grained closure of both hierarchies of Section 2 at once.

12.2 The gradient expansion and the counterterm

Nobody can compute from first principles: the short modes have shell-crossed and are genuinely non-perturbative. EFT does not try. It writes the most general expression allowed by symmetry (rotations, the equivalence principle) in terms of the long-wavelength fields, ordered in derivatives:

The first term is a pressure, the next two are bulk and shear viscosities — the same structure as Navier–Stokes (Appendix A.5) — and is a stochastic term, uncorrelated with the long modes, that represents the particular configuration of small-scale structure. To leading order the deterministic terms collapse into a single coefficient, and the one-loop power spectrum acquires the counterterm

with (here absorbing growth factors and ) measured rather than derived. The counterterm also cancels the cut-off dependence of the loop integral: what one loop gets wrong on short scales, absorbs.

Chapman–Enskog (Section 5)EFT of large-scale structure
Expansion parameterKnudsen number
Microscopic dynamics below the cut-offCollisions: simple, knownShell-crossed halos: non-perturbative
First-order termsViscosity , conductivity , ,
CoefficientsDerived from the collision operatorMeasured from simulations or data
Higher ordersBurnett: unstable, rarely usedTwo-loop plus higher-derivative counterterms: systematic
Stochastic termThermal fluctuations, negligible: essential, behaves like noise
Where it fails: the scrape-off layer: inside halos

In this sense Navier–Stokes is itself the effective field theory of the Boltzmann equation, and MHD and gyrokinetics are effective theories of the kinetic equations below their own cut-offs. EFT is less a new rung of the ladder than the general rule for building every rung above Vlasov.

12.3 A worked example in one dimension

One-dimensional cold dark matter is a set of parallel sheets, and its gravity can be computed exactly even after the sheets cross. In an Einstein–de Sitter universe with the scale factor as the clock, each sheet obeys

where is the Lagrangian position the sheet would have if the sheets were still in order. Before crossing, and the Zel’dovich solution is exact: it is the single-stream, pressureless closure of Section 7, case one. After crossing it lets streams pass straight through each other, while real gravity folds them into halos:

Evolve both from the same initial conditions in 24 boxes and compare power spectra. The difference grows exactly as on large scales. Fitting the single counterterm for cuts the error of Zel’dovich from 1.1% to 0.2% there, and roughly halves it out to (9.6% → 4.4%). Beyond that, near , the expansion fails, as any expansion must.

The fitted comes out negative in this convention. Zel’dovich over-disperses matter by letting streams fly apart; real gravity holds them in halos, so the short modes act on the long ones like a negative pressure, adding power back.

12.4 Two ways to confront EFT with data

The n-point route (statistics level). Compress the field into summary statistics — the power spectrum, bispectrum, their redshift-space multipoles — and fit the analytic EFT predictions with a Gaussian likelihood:

This is the standard, mature route: it has been used to analyse galaxy surveys with public codes such as CLASS-PT, PyBird and velocileptors. Its limits are information beyond two or three points, the covariance , and the choice of .

The field-level route. Instead of compressing, forward-model the whole field. Given initial modes , an EFT forward model (perturbative or Lagrangian, plus counterterms and bias) predicts the late-time field mode by mode, and the likelihood compares fields, phases included:

The initial modes are sampled along with the parameters (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with millions of variables), which is why differentiable forward models such as pmwd and JaxPM matter. Two things change. The noise in the likelihood is no longer cosmic variance but only the stochastic term ; and the deterministic counterterm and the stochastic term are separated, where the power spectrum lumps them together.

The 1D boxes let us test both claims honestly, using the same modes :

The two routes give consistent coefficients, but here the field level does not win on precision. Mode by mode, only about 22% of the difference between the exact and Zel’dovich fields is the deterministic term; the rest is stochastic, and cosmic-variance cancellation cannot remove noise that is genuinely there. The gain of the field level is therefore not automatic: it grows as the forward model improves and the stochastic term shrinks (better perturbative or Lagrangian models, larger scales, lower shot noise). What the field level does deliver even here is the separation: pooled over all boxes it measures the deterministic response , distinct from the that the power spectrum absorbs once stochastic and cross terms are folded in.

12.4b A field-level test in two dimensions

The 1D test left an open question: does the field level pay off once the forward model is good enough? Two dimensions answer it. A particle-mesh simulation of cold dark matter in a periodic 2D box (2562 particles and cells, Einstein–de Sitter, 8 independent boxes, rms linear density contrast about 1 today) is compared with two perturbative forward models built from the same initial modes:

On top of each, the leading counterterm is fitted below a cut-off , mode by mode and with phases, for , and, for comparison, from each box’s power spectrum.

The error power is the field-level figure of merit: it asks how well the model reproduces this universe, not just its statistics. 2LPT cuts it by an order of magnitude on large scales relative to Zel’dovich, and the counterterm lowers it further inside the fit range for 2LPT, but hardly at all for Zel’dovich, whose residual is dominated by second-order terms it does not contain.

This is the answer to the 1D puzzle. With Zel’dovich as the forward model only 1% of the large-scale residual is the deterministic counterterm, so the field-level estimate of is no better than the n-point one (both scatter by about their own size). With 2LPT the deterministic share rises to 34%, and the field-level estimate, per box, is 1.3× tighter than the n-point estimate, , from exactly the same modes. The gain is modest at this resolution and amplitude, and it is bought with the forward model: the better it captures the deterministic nonlinear evolution, the more of the residual is signal rather than noise.

Reproduce with sims/eft_2d_field_level.py (about 20 seconds; --ng and --nbox scale it up).

12.5 Where PINNs can change the results — and where they cannot

  • Little impact on the n-point route. The EFT prediction is analytic in Fourier space; fitting is a cheap linear or likelihood fit with no PDE to solve. A PINN adds cost, not information. The machine-learning gain there comes from emulators that make loop integrals fast inside a sampler.
  • Learning the closure as a function, at the field level. Given smoothed simulation fields and , the smoothed continuity and Euler equations of 12.1 hold point by point. A PINN can represent the fields and an unknown stress (or , ) and train on the residuals:
    This is the Grad–Shafranov and Alfvén strategy of Section 11 applied to cosmology: the equations fix what the data cannot, and time- or scale-dependence of the coefficients comes for free.
  • Sparse and noisy tracers. Galaxies sample the density and velocity sparsely. A PINN reconstruction that enforces continuity and the Euler equation everywhere can interpolate between tracers physically, which matters for velocity reconstruction and for fields that are never observed directly.
  • The main risk: absorbing the physics into the network. A flexible network can mimic a counterterm, a bias term or a cosmological-parameter shift. If the PINN’s freedom overlaps with the EFT terms, the coefficients become degenerate with the network weights and cosmological parameters can be biased without any sign of trouble in the loss. The protection is to keep the EFT structure explicit — let the network represent fields, not the closure, unless the closure is the target — to validate on simulations with known answers, and to propagate uncertainty (ensembles or Bayesian PINNs). Section 11’s caveats also apply: shocks and multi-streaming are exactly where networks struggle.

The honest summary: for summary statistics, analytic EFT plus emulators is the right tool. At the field level, where the closure is a PDE evaluated on data, PINNs are a natural way to learn the closure, provided its form is kept explicit so that what the network learns is physics rather than a fit.

Reproduce the figures in this section with sims/eft_1d.py (about 30 seconds).

13The pattern

Read the table across any row and the three fields look different. Read it down and they are the same story told three times.

Each field begins with an exact, reversible, uncomputable description. Each reorganises it into a hierarchy that is still exact and still uncomputable. Each closes the hierarchy with an assumption that cannot be derived, and thereby acquires both tractability and an arrow of time. Each then discovers a region — the collapsing halo, the divertor, the cluster core — where the closure has no justification and where, inconveniently, all the interesting physics lives. And each now uses direct kinetic simulation to test and calibrate its reduced models, which remain the workhorses for design and interpretation.

The differences that matter are few: whether the force screens, whether the source has one sign or two, how many particles there are, and whether an external field imposes a preferred direction. Those four facts determine whether you need a tree, whether collisions are physics or numerical noise, how many transport coefficients you have, and where your closure will fail.

Worth remembering

Collisionality is not a property of a force law. It is a ratio of timescales — which is why unscreened gravity is collisionless in a galaxy and collisional in a star cluster, and why screened Coulomb interaction is collisionless in a tokamak core and collisional two metres away in its divertor.

AAppendix: derivations

The steps the main text skips, in the order they are used. Each is short enough to check by hand.

A.1 From Liouville to the first BBGKY equation

Write the Liouville equation of Section 1 in velocities, with the pair force on particle from particle :

Multiply by and integrate over . Every term with is a total derivative in or (the force on particle does not depend on ), so it integrates to zero because vanishes at infinity or is periodic. What survives is the term. Its pair-force part has identical contributions, one from each partner , and , so

This is the equation quoted in Section 4. Integrating instead over gives the -th member, which always contains on the right: that is the whole BBGKY hierarchy.

A.2 The mean field and the Vlasov equation

Insert . In the product term the integral is just the density, , so

Moving it to the left gives the streaming operator with the total smooth force . The remaining term is the collision operator . Setting removes it, leaving the Vlasov equation. For gravity, , the mean force is with , because is the Green’s function of the Laplacian.

A.3 Fokker–Planck from the master equation, and the Coulomb logarithm

Start from the exact master form of the collision term, with the rate of kicks suffered by a particle of velocity :

If kicks are small, Taylor-expand the first term in its first argument (not in the kick itself):

The zeroth-order term cancels the loss term. Integrating over and pulling the derivatives outside gives

A.9 Why leapfrog is symplectic

Split . The kick is the exact flow of alone, and the drift is the exact flow of alone. Each is a canonical map, so each preserves phase-space volume, and so does their composition. Kick–drift–kick is therefore an exact solution of a nearby “shadow” Hamiltonian , which is why its energy error oscillates instead of drifting over millions of steps.
